Sven Hedin (1865 to 1952) was a Swedish explorer who mapped large parts of Central Asia and Tibet. On four expeditions between 1893 and 1935 he crossed the Taklamakan desert, nearly dying of thirst in 1895, mapped the wandering lake of Lop Nur, and in 1900 found the ruined town of Loulan, a Silk Road outpost abandoned since about the 4th century.

In Tibet he traced the sources of the Indus, Brahmaputra and Sutlej and mapped the Transhimalaya range. His travel books, illustrated with his own drawings, made him world famous. From 1927 to 1935 he led the Sino-Swedish Expedition, a joint venture with Chinese scientists across Inner Mongolia and Xinjiang.

His reputation fell over his politics. He backed Germany in the First World War, and in the 1930s and 1940s he admired Hitler and spoke for the Nazi regime. He was the last Swede to be made a noble, in 1902. Compare Aurel Stein, who worked the same deserts for Britain.
